eligibility_reason: A pre-registered, high-powered registered report (N = 1,459 MTurk US workers, new data) whose classic-ISE conditions follow Thürmer & McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) 'very closely' and whose pure-bystander conditions re-test the bystander ISE of Sutton et al. (2006); the authors frame it as 'confirming its replicability' and state their classic-ISE results 'mirror those of existing research (Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, Experiment 3)'. The paper also has new theory-testing aims (behavioural bystander ISE), which get no entry.

effects.original_title: Beyond motivated reasoning: Hostile reactions to critical comments from the outgroup
effects.original_authors: Thürmer, J. Lukas; McCrea, Sean M.
effects.outcome: Defensive response to criticism of the ingroup: bonus (0-12 cents) awarded to the commenter at a cost to the participant (primary, behavioural ISE), plus self-reported message motive (constructiveness) and message threat
effects.contrast: Criticism of the ingroup (Americans) from an ingroup (US) source vs an outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 1)
effects.description: Experiment 3 of Thürmer & McCrea (2018) found that US participants responded more defensively to criticism of Americans from a Singapore (outgroup) commenter than from a US (ingroup) commenter, withholding more of a costly bonus from the outgroup critic (behavioural intergroup sensitivity effect) and rating the outgroup critic's comment as less constructive and more threatening.
effects.citation_sentence: To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely. We used the same established manipulation for the classic ISE, self-report measures that are used widely in ISE research (Hornsey & Imani, 2004), and the same behavioural measure.
effects.evidence: Results 4.3.1 (p. 6-7): 'In line with our prediction, Contrast 1 was significant, t(1,455) = -4.503, p < .001, r = .117, indicating a behavioural classic ISE.' ... 'Contrast 1 was significant for message motive, t(1,455) = -15.104, p < .001, r = .369, and for message threat, t(1,455) = 7.081, p < .001, r = .183.' Discussion (p. 9): 'Registered analyses revealed strong evidence for the classic ISE across behavioural and self-report measures'. Limitations (p. 10): 'the classic ISE paradigm (i.e., the US and Singapore conditions) was adapted from and results mirror those of existing research (Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, Experiment 3).'
effects.notes: Self-replication (same authors). Merged in pass 2 from pass-1 rows s1:classic_ise_behavioural and s1:classic_ise_selfreport: under the codebook, several measures of the same claim within one study are one entry, and the self-report and behavioural tests are measures of one classic-ISE contrast taken from the same original experiment. A coder who treats the self-report ISE (classic Hornsey-style finding; items 'directly adapted from Hornsey and Imani (2004)', https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167203261295) as a claim separate from T&M's behavioural ISE would split this into two rows; both would be success. Type: same manipulation, same behavioural measure, same population (CloudResearch MTurk US), procedure followed 'very closely'; deliberate changes were added bystander cells, motive measured before threat, and an identification measure added after the DV — close experiment is plausible; tiebreaker (direct vs close -> direct) applied. Exploratory Johnson-Neyman analyses show the behavioural classic ISE only at identification >= 2.45, but the registered contrast is significant and the authors 'establish the ISE as an empirical fact'. Author first names taken from this paper's byline (same authors).

effects.original_title: Reactions to internal and external criticism of outgroups: Social convention in the intergroup sensitivity effect
effects.original_authors: Sutton, R.; Elder, T.; Douglas, K.
effects.outcome: Self-reported message motive (constructiveness) and message threat ratings of criticism directed at an uninvolved outgroup
effects.contrast: Criticism of an outgroup (South Africans) from a same-group (South African) source vs a different-outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 2, pure bystander ISE)
effects.description: Uninvolved bystanders (members of a third group) also show the intergroup sensitivity effect, judging criticism of a group more negatively when it comes from an outsider than from a member of the criticized group.
effects.citation_sentence: In line with this general norm explanation, Sutton et al. (2006) observed the ISE even among uninvolved bystanders who were members of a third group (bystander ISE). ... For the bystander ISE, the involvement of the ingroup can vary: Sutton et al. (2006) compared criticism between two outgroups (in our terminology Outgroup A and Outgroup B), where the ingroup is neither the target nor the source of criticism. We thus term the resulting effect the pure bystander effect.
effects.evidence: Results 4.3.2 (p. 7): 'As predicted, a bystander ISE (Contrast 2) emerged for the self-report measures of message motive, t(1,455) = -20.208, p < .001, r = .469, and message threat, t(1,455) = 13.341, p < .001, r = .331. Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006), participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by between-group criticism than within-group criticism.' Discussion: 'we also found unequivocal support for the bystander ISE in self-reports.'
effects.notes: Kept despite neither candidate coding it (luna56 calls the bystander ISE 'a newly added extension rather than a separately replicated original effect'). The source supports an entry: Sutton et al. (2006) published the pure-bystander finding (criticism between two outgroups), this study re-tests exactly that contrast on self-report with new participants, and the authors report it as 'Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006)'. What is new here is the behavioural bystander test, which gets no row. Ambiguity concerns eligibility/type more than result: the test is framed as a theory test of the norm account, not called a replication. Type: different groups (US participants judging South Africa vs Singapore) and Thürmer & McCrea materials rather than Sutton et al.'s, so close extension (conceptual possible). Author first names not given in the paper. NOT coded: behavioural bystander ISE (no prior claim; the authors predicted its absence); Comparison I vs Sutton et al. (2008, book chapter) 'similar magnitude' (exploratory; bystander ISE larger here); exploratory moderation by identification 'in line with' Thürmer et al. (2019); serial mediation 'confirmed past theorizing'; Source and Target contrasts (new exploratory).

ling26:10.1002--ejsp.2748#ling26:9ea9577.reason: Same original (Thürmer & McCrea 2018, Exp. 3, doi 10.1037/mot0000097) and same classic-ISE contrast (ingroup target, ingroup vs outgroup source), success. Its replication_type 'close experiment' differs from my 'direct' (tiebreaker direct vs close -> direct).

luna56:10.1002--ejsp.2748#luna56:ac8edfe.reason: Same original and the same classic-ISE claim (defensive response to outgroup vs ingroup criticism of the ingroup), success, direct. Its view that the pure bystander ISE is not a replicated effect is not adopted: Sutton et al. (2006) published that finding and it is re-tested here (s1:bystander_ise_selfreport).
